brief.head: Museum homework
brief.text: Before each mu­seum in Spain, Amit Varma asked ChatGPT Deep Research for an art-history les­son. Soon he could roughly guess the year of a Velázquez paint­ing. {097-S01}

brief.head: Why context counts
brief.text: Nomsita asked whether art should not stand on its own. It should, Amit Varma said, but the artist’s jour­ney and the fer­ment of the times deepen ap­pre­ci­a­tion. {097-C03}

brief.head: The prolific privilege
brief.text: Pablo Picasso may have painted more than any painter ever, Amit Varma said, be­cause suc­cess let him keep going. Unsuccessful painters even­tu­ally quit for some­thing else. {097-C13}

brief.head: Genius at Starbucks
brief.text: Picasso’s café cir­cle in Paris, Amit Varma said, was like the great­est minds of the age gath­er­ing at your local BKC Starbucks, un­recog­nised until much later. {097-J09}

brief.head: A page a day
brief.text: Amit Varma’s first must-read is EH Gombrich’s *The Story of Art*, which goes paint­ing by paint­ing. Read a page a day, he said, and it will ex­pand your brain. {097-R21}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: It takes a long time to grow young.
thought.who: Pablo Picasso, quoted by Amit Varma as a philosophy of ageing

lead.kicker: Amit Varma’s Spanish holiday, and what it taught him
lead.head: Old masters, new tricks

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 97

body: Amit Varma spent fif­teen days in Spain, walk­ing about eight kilo­me­tres a day and giv­ing him­self an ed­u­ca­tion in art. He came home with a the­sis about old age.

He had looked hard­est at five Spanish painters: Diego Velázquez, Francisco Goya, Pablo Picasso, Joan Miró and Salvador Dali. All were na­tional icons by their thir­ties, yet the work that spoke to him most came in their fifties to eight­ies.

“All five of them, in my opin­ion, did their great­est work when they were re­ally old, when they had no need to even try new things,” Varma told Ajay Shah. “But they kept rein­vent­ing them­selves.” {097-C01}
Most peo­ple who reach such a peak, he said, coast on their past glo­ries and rarely rock the boat for fear of los­ing their fans.
Varma set this against the myth of youth­ful ge­nius: Kurt Cobain’s line that it is bet­ter to burn out than to fade away, and the rock mu­si­cians who died at 27.
At 21, Varma ad­mit­ted, he fan­ta­sised about dying at 27 after achiev­ing some­thing great. “I achieved noth­ing great, so I post­poned it.” {097-J01}
Shah and Susan had planned to do cool things by 29 and then give up. Then 29 came along, and, Shah said, “we set­tled into a marathon.”
## Craft first, art later
A teenage gui­tar prodigy can play Eddie Van Halen licks per­fectly, Varma said. The craft is all there. “Does the art come now? The art doesn’t quite come now.” {097-C02}
Varma linked the art to thehraav, a set­tled­ness that comes with age.

Velázquez painted *Las Meninas* at 57. Goya, deaf and in his late sev­en­ties, cov­ered the walls of his house with dark mu­rals and told no one. Picasso, at 75, painted 58 ver­sions of *Las Meninas*. Miró, in his eight­ies, said he was paint­ing for the young of the fu­ture.
Goya, paint­ing for no one, moved Varma al­most as much by that free­dom as by the work it­self.
## Never too late
Varma read out Picasso’s line that one starts to get young at sixty, “and then it’s too late”. With longer life­spans, he told the 59-year-old Shah, it no longer is.

His mes­sage was for the 45-year-old stuck in a bank­ing job who thinks he could have been a writer or a mu­si­cian. “Could is not the word, can is the word,” Varma said. “It is never too late.” {097-C14}
This was no dis­dain for youth, he added, though he doubted Wim Wenders could have made *Perfect Days* in his thir­ties.
## The economist’s view

In fi­nite fields such as chess, math­e­mat­ics and the­o­ret­i­cal physics, Shah said, peo­ple peak in their twen­ties to for­ties; econ­o­mists peak in their for­ties to six­ties. “The peak time for a CEO is the fifties. The per­fect age for a founder in a startup is fifty,” he said. {097-C15} Fifty years of ev­i­dence show all these ages ris­ing.
Longer healthspans are one rea­son, Shah said. Another is a re­search ma­chine of PhDs, jour­nals and grants that sets peo­ple free ever later.
What older minds do best, he ar­gued, is in­te­gra­tion: see­ing the big pic­ture across many per­spec­tives, while the young write sharp, clean, cute code.
Varma turned the the­sis on his co-host: that wis­dom, he said, could not have come from the twenty-year-old Ajay Shah. Shah agreed: “Absolutely.”
By then the light had gone. “I don’t even know if I’m vis­i­ble any­more,” Varma said.

second.label: Bob Dylan at 56
second.head: Elvis would have to wait
second.deck: A brush with death, survived, gave Amit Varma his favourite Dylan album

pic.caption: Bob Dylan at Nowlan Park, Kilkenny, in 2019

body: At 56, Bob Dylan was in hos­pi­tal with peri­cardi­tis and thought he was going to die. {097-S09} He even gave a quote, as Amit Varma told it: “I think I’m going to see Elvis soon.” {097-J14}

He sur­vived, and that year made *Time Out of Mind*, Varma’s favourite Dylan album. Its song *Not Dark Yet* has the lines: “Sometimes my bur­den is more than I can bear. It’s not dark yet, but it’s get­ting there.” {097-R14}

It is a pe­riod, Varma noted, that the Dylan biopic won’t show. He raised it just after re­call­ing how fans branded Dylan a Judas for going elec­tric: they had come for the pho­to­graph Dylan left of him­self, not the man.

quote.text: Dylan writes this when he’s in hos­pi­tal ear­lier that year with peri­cardi­tis, and he thinks he’s going to die.

third.head: Too real for the Pope

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Pope’s unflattering portrait

body: A court painter was ex­pected to flat­ter his pa­trons, Amit Varma said. Diego Velázquez kept going a lit­tle be­yond that.
Court tra­di­tion painted the royal buf­foons and dwarfs as car­i­ca­tures. Velázquez painted one dwarf as a learned, thought­ful man.

In 1650, at 51, he painted Pope Innocent the Fifth, if Varma re­mem­bered cor­rectly. The Pope hated it, be­cause it was too real. {097-S03} “A painter is not just pick­ing up what he sees in front of him,” Varma said, “but also telling a deeper truth that he might be able to per­ceive.”

He painted the writ­ers Aesop and Menippus as beg­gars, and Varma has stood be­fore both at the Prado. {#aesop} By then, Varma said, “he’s not hint­ing at depths. He’s ac­tu­ally telling you sto­ries.”

box.title: Three museums, one education
box.text: Madrid’s Prado runs from the Renaissance to Goya; the Reina Sofía holds mod­ern art and a lot of Picasso; the Thyssen gives much of the twen­ti­eth cen­tury, pop art in­cluded. With con­text, Amit Varma said, it is a full ed­u­ca­tion in art. {#museums}

sections.label: The first master
sections.head: Only you shall paint me
sections.caption: Velázquez and Las Meninas
body: Diego Velázquez was born in 1599, Amit Varma said, into a world with no cin­ema, few books and no way of see­ing most of the art made be­fore him. {#velazquez}

His teacher, Pacheco, was a medi­ocre re­al­ist who trained him in the clas­sics. Yet at 19 Velázquez painted *Old Woman Frying Eggs*, and at 20 *The Waterseller of Seville*, hint­ing at depths be­yond what was in front of him.
There was no art mar­ket, only royal pa­tron­age. In 1624, at about 25, he was sum­moned by King Philip IV, who loved his por­trait and de­creed that only Velázquez would paint him. {097-S02}
He kept seek­ing in­flu­ences: time with Rubens in 1628, then a year and a half in Italy from 1629.
## A can­vas to walk into
*Las Meninas*, painted in 1656 when he was 57, is his most pow­er­ful work. Standing be­fore it, Varma felt he could walk into it. {097-S04}

There is an open door at the back, light from the right, and a dis­tant mir­ror hold­ing the royal cou­ple, who may be stand­ing where we are. Velázquez painted him­self at work. It is, Varma said, “much more enig­matic than that fa­mous enig­matic Mona Lisa”. {097-J06}
Goya called Velázquez the only artist worth im­i­tat­ing, and Picasso sat at the Prado copy­ing both. {#prado}
~ For Varma it was the first sign of his the­sis: tech­nique had be­come sec­ond na­ture, and “there he is now play­ing at an­other level”.

quote.text: Not ex­clu­sively mine, as in you’re only going to paint me, but only you are going to paint me. I am ex­clu­sively yours

sections.label: The second master
sections.head: Deaf ears, open eyes
sections.caption: Goya’s deafness and dark satire
body: Francisco Goya be­came a court painter young, Amit Varma said, like his hero Velázquez. Then, at 47, he went deaf. {#goyadeaf}

By 1797 or 1798 he had pro­duced *Los Caprichos*, satir­i­cal etch­ings drawn, in Goya’s words, from “the mul­ti­tudes of faults and vices com­mon in every civil so­ci­ety”. *He Broke the Jug* shows chil­dren being beaten. Perhaps Varma’s favourite is *The Dream of Reason Produces Monsters*, which Goya meant as the cover.
In 1800 Charles IV com­mis­sioned a fam­ily por­trait. Goya made the roy­als look like “weird peo­ple with their own in­ter­nal dra­mas”, and painted him­self paint­ing them, a nod to *Las Meninas*.
## Stolen, then owned

His 1808 ex­e­cu­tion scene, with face­less French sol­diers and a lantern light­ing the man in the white shirt, resur­faces in Picasso’s *Guernica* and *Massacre in Korea*. Critics dis­like the lat­ter; Varma calls it a mas­ter­piece. {097-R07}
Varma saw in it the truth of Picasso’s maxim that good artists bor­row and great artists steal. Stealing is not dis­hon­ourable, he said: it means mak­ing some­thing com­pletely your own. {097-C04}

~ Ajay Shah re­called John Maynard Keynes call­ing Newton not just the first of the sci­en­tists but the last of the ma­gi­cians. Varma saw Goya the same way: the last of the old mas­ters and the first of the mod­erns, a bridge be­tween worlds like Istanbul. {097-C05}

quote.text: To steal in terms of art is to make some­thing your own.

sections.label: The third master
sections.head: The long road to childhood
sections.caption: Picasso’s late playfulness
body: Pablo Picasso was mas­ter­ing clas­si­cal paint­ing at 15 and 16, Amit Varma said, and would be a leg­end had he died after Cubism. What moved Varma most was what came later.
He read Picasso’s late say­ings as a phi­los­o­phy of age­ing. You mas­ter tech­nique young, then spend a life­time learn­ing to drop it and play like a child. {097-C07}
Picasso called his work a way of keep­ing a diary, and said he was al­ways doing what he could not yet do, in order to learn how.
## Prisoners of the hit
Varma com­pared it with music. Once a song be­comes fa­mous, he said, a mu­si­cian is tied to it, and spends the rest of his life cov­er­ing his younger self. {097-C09}
U2, in rel­a­tively old age, came out with a whole bunch of cover ver­sions of their own songs. {#u2}

Picasso painted until he died in his late eight­ies, and much of it was shown only after his death. Varma had no pa­tience for the crit­ics who sneered at it. Of *Self Portrait Facing Death* he asked: “Is this not ge­nius? Is this not mas­ter­ful?” {097-R08}
~ Late bloomers, Varma joked, feed his Bengali pro­cras­ti­na­tion: he can waste twenty more years, and do his best work at 70 or 80. {097-J13}

quote.text: When I was young I could draw like Rafael. But it has taken me a life­time to draw like a child.
quote.who: Pablo Picasso, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: The fourth master
sections.head: A single line, years long
sections.caption: Miró’s stripped-down canvases
body: Joan Miró, Amit Varma said, wanted to get past the clichés of how things are de­picted, to­wards the es­sen­tial. He thought in terms of po­etry and music.
A mu­si­cian can­not ex­plain why a set of notes makes you cry, and nei­ther can you. “Sometimes we de­mand too much ex­pla­na­tion from artists,” Varma said. {097-C11}
## Rooms of al­most noth­ing
At the Fundació Joan Miró in Barcelona he stood in a room of large can­vases that were a sin­gle line, or a sin­gle blotch of colour. *Blue I*, *II* and *III* were painted when Miró was 65. {#blue}
“It took me only a mo­ment to draw this line with a brush,” Miró said of one, “but it took me months, per­haps even years of re­flec­tion to form the idea of it.” {097-C12}
Peers and crit­ics said such work was easy to par­ody. In his eight­ies, Miró an­swered that he was paint­ing not for them but for the young of the fu­ture. {097-S11}
~ His rule for stay­ing alive as an artist, which Varma read out, was to al­ways work against your­self and de­stroy your past ac­com­plish­ments. {097-C10}

quote.text: I’m not paint­ing for you guys. I’m paint­ing for the young of the fu­ture. I want my work to in­spire them.

sections.label: More late mastery
sections.head: Late starters, longer runs
sections.caption: late bloomers and the rising peak age
body: Some artists mas­ter their craft young and keep going; oth­ers start late, Amit Varma said. Penelope Fitzgerald wrote her first novel after 60. {097-R16}
His favourite of hers, *The Gate of Angels*, was writ­ten in her mid-seventies. {#gate}

Beethoven went deaf around the same time as Goya, and wrote his fa­mous string quar­tets after ten years or more of deaf­ness. “The din from out­side is gone, but there is a din from in­side,” Varma said. {097-S12}
## Two forces

Ajay Shah said peak ages dif­fer by field, early in chess and later for startup founders, at about fifty, and that all have been ris­ing. One force is good news: longer healthspans let peo­ple keep pil­ing up knowl­edge across fields.

The other is bad news. Science has be­come a busi­ness of PhDs, pub­lish­ing, jour­nal ed­i­tors and grants, and the age at which re­searchers win their first grant keeps ris­ing. “At the point where a per­son first gets funded is re­ally the point at which they get free,” Shah said. {097-C16}
His ideal is to give bril­liant young peo­ple au­ton­omy early, and long healthspans as well.
~ Older peo­ple, Shah ar­gued, should change the na­ture of their work: from a young programmer’s cute code to see­ing the big pic­ture and in­te­grat­ing knowl­edge. {097-C17}

quote.text: One deep thing that comes as peo­ple get older is in­ter­dis­ci­plinar­ity. You get to know many, many per­spec­tives.
How can you be a hun­dred years be­fore your time? Like you make so much pos­si­ble by just doing that, by show­ing that it’s okay, you have per­mis­sion to think in this way.

p3.title: Tales from the galleries
p3.deck: Secret murals, a costly bolt, a prank that wasn’t, and Velázquez revisited

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the murals Goya painted for nobody
stories.head: What Goya kept to himself
body: Francisco Goya moved into a house called the Abode of the Deaf, Amit Varma said, after its pre­vi­ous owner, who was also deaf.

In his late sev­en­ties and grap­pling with mor­tal­ity, he painted ex­tremely dark mu­rals on its walls. He never men­tioned them to any­one. They were found after his death, and some­one had the good sense to use a newly in­vented tech­nique to lift them from the plas­ter.

They were not his only hid­den work. *The Disasters of War*, etch­ings with ti­tles like *Bury Them and Stay Silent*, went un­seen for decades. They made Varma think of the Japanese artist Yoshihiro Tatsumi’s *The Push Man and Other Stories*. {097-R11}
Today the Black Paintings hang to­gether in one room at the Prado: four­teen of them, though some say a fif­teenth is some­where in America. {#fourteen}
Varma spent half an hour there. He had al­most left the build­ing when he de­cided he wanted to go back. {097-R04}

The fa­mous *Saturn Devouring His Son* moved him least, per­haps be­cause he had seen it re­pro­duced so often. His favourite is *The Dog*. Goya ti­tled none of the paint­ings, and noth­ing about this one is ex­plained. Is the mass at the bot­tom mud, or water? “Is it ex­is­ten­tial angst? We re­ally don’t know what’s hap­pen­ing.”

~ Goya, Varma said, was decades ahead of ev­ery­one, an­tic­i­pat­ing the Impressionists and the Surrealists. What moved him al­most as much was the se­crecy. “He’s just doing it for the doing of them.” {097-S06}
stories.why: Goya made his dark­est work for no au­di­ence at all. Free of any need for ap­proval, the deaf old painter got decades ahead of his time, and the work be­came its own rea­son. {097-C06}
stories.postscript: Were it not for Picasso, Varma said, Goya might be his favourite painter of all time.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Goya’s Black Paintings

stories.kicker: Amit Varma in a room at the Picasso Museum, Barcelona
stories.head: One painting, fifty-eight times
body: *Las Meninas* had dev­as­tated Pablo Picasso when he first saw it as a young man. In 1957, at 75, he went back to it and painted his own ver­sions: 58 of them.

They hang in one room of the Picasso Museum in Barcelona, or­dered by date. Large can­vases are dated a day apart, and on one wall four were made on the same day. Amit Varma could not re­mem­ber the exact dates, but the pace as­ton­ished him.
Varma watched a cou­ple of vis­i­tors move past them at full speed in the op­po­site di­rec­tion, not un­der­stand­ing what was going on. {097-S08}
~ Picasso was not try­ing to get it right, Varma said, “be­cause there is no right”. Velázquez him­self would have ac­cepted that. {097-C08}
stories.why: One old mas­ter played with another’s late mas­ter­piece. Picasso called his work a way of keep­ing a diary; seen in date order, the 58 can­vases are a record of him grow­ing day by day.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Picasso’s fifty-eight Las Meninas

stories.kicker: A factory tale Amit Varma told to explain Miró
stories.head: Seventy years in a screwdriver
body: Something went wrong in a fac­tory Henry Ford was run­ning, Amit Varma said, and his best en­gi­neers could not fix it. So Ford called in the fore­most man in the field, aged sev­enty or so.
The ex­pert walked around, put his ear to some­thing and did some tap­ping. Then he asked for a screw­driver, took out a bolt, moved some­thing in­side and put it back. Everything worked again.

Varma for­got the exact fee: “Let us say for now that it was eighty thou­sand dol­lars.” Ford asked for a break­down. Item one was a dol­lar for chang­ing the bolt. Item two was the rest, “for the sev­enty years in which I learned what to look for”. {097-S10}
~ Varma told it be­side a line from Joan Miró: a stroke took a mo­ment to draw, but years of re­flec­tion to con­ceive. {097-C12}
stories.why: Mastery is mostly in­vis­i­ble. The sim­ple ges­ture of an old hand holds decades of judge­ment, and that judge­ment is what the in­voice charged for. The same holds for a sin­gle line on a vast can­vas.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Henry Ford’s seventy-year invoice

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Picasso’s search for a new language
stories.head: Matisse checks the calendar
body: At 15 and 16, Pablo Picasso was al­ready a mas­ter of clas­si­cal paint­ing. As a teenager in Barcelona he hung out at the café Els Quatre Gats, even de­sign­ing its menu, be­fore leav­ing for Paris.
In 1901 a close friend shot him­self, and Picasso sank into his Blue Period; the Rose Period fol­lowed. Then he and his café cir­cle tired of re­al­ism and every ism since.

African tribal art led Picasso to *Les Demoiselles d’Avignon*, around 1907. Henri Matisse, whom he ad­mired, thought it a prank. Had Matisse owned a Garmin watch, Amit Varma joked, he would have checked whether it was April 1. {097-J07}
~ Braque saw what Picasso was doing, and the two built Cubism to­gether with­out a hint of ri­valry. {097-S07} They moved from an­a­lytic Cubism to syn­thetic.

quote.text: But there are other peo­ple who are like, yeah, boss, I see what you’re doing.

stories.postscript: After the First World War, Picasso turned back to neo­clas­si­cism: fa­mous for Cubism, Varma said, but not tied to it.

quiz.q: Which tool did Amit Varma use to prepare for each museum he visited in Spain?
quiz.a: ChatGPT Deep Research, which wrote him a nar­ra­tive art-history les­son for each.

quiz.q: Why did Pope Innocent hate the portrait Velázquez painted of him in 1650?
quiz.a: He said it was too real: Velázquez painted him as he saw him.

quiz.q: Where did Goya paint his Black Paintings, and who knew about them?
quiz.a: On the walls of his house; he told no­body, and they sur­faced after his death.

quiz.q: What did Henri Matisse make of Picasso’s *Les Demoiselles d’Avignon* when he first saw it?
quiz.a: He thought it was a prank, a joke that could not pos­si­bly be se­ri­ous.

quiz.q: At what age did Penelope Fitzgerald write her first novel, according to Amit Varma?
quiz.a: After sixty; *The Gate of Angels* came in her mid-seventies.

quiz.q: According to Ajay Shah, at what point does a young researcher really become free?
quiz.a: When they first get funded; oth­er­wise they work in some­one else’s lab.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 97. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Pablo Picasso (Argentina. Revista Vea y Lea, public domain); Francisco Goya (Vicente López Portaña, public domain); Bob Dylan (Raph_PH, CC BY 2.0); Diego Velázquez (Diego Velázquez, public domain); Joan Miró (Carl Van Vechten, public domain); Ludwig van Beethoven (Joseph Karl Stieler, public domain); Ernst Gombrich (Bert Verhoeff for Anefo, CC0); Wim Wenders (Martin Kraft, CC BY-SA 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Apple, Spotify and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: ChatGPT Deep Research
shelf.creator: OpenAI
shelf.why: Amit calls it ‘off the charts good’: it asks clar­i­fy­ing ques­tions, cites sources and writes deep cus­tom re­ports, and has re­placed Google for him, down to build­ing an art-history guide to each mu­seum he vis­ited.

shelf.title: The Prado, Reina Sofía and Thyssen museums, Madrid
shelf.why: They cover dif­fer­ent eras: the Prado runs from the Renaissance to Goya, the Reina Sofía has mod­ern art and lots of Picasso, and the Thyssen cov­ers much of the 20th cen­tury, in­clud­ing pop art.

shelf.title: Las Meninas
shelf.creator: Diego Velázquez
shelf.why: Its depth, light, mir­ror and self-portrait of the painter make it more enig­matic than the Mona Lisa.

shelf.title: The Black Paintings (especially The Dog)
shelf.creator: Francisco Goya
shelf.why: Amit calls the half hour he spent there an emo­tion­ally mov­ing ex­pe­ri­ence and went back for more.

shelf.title: Los Caprichos (especially The Dream of Reason Produces Monsters)
shelf.creator: Francisco Goya
shelf.why: They are dark, so­cially pierc­ing work, and The Dream of Reason Produces Monsters is per­haps Amit’s favourite sin­gle Goya work.

shelf.title: Picasso’s Las Meninas series
shelf.creator: Pablo Picasso
shelf.why: Seen in chrono­log­i­cal order, they show an old mas­ter play­ing and grow­ing day by day.

shelf.title: Massacre in Korea
shelf.creator: Pablo Picasso
shelf.why: Critics don’t rate it, but Amit calls it a mas­ter­piece.

shelf.title: Self Portrait Facing Death
shelf.creator: Pablo Picasso
shelf.why: Amit finds it ‘genius’ and ‘masterful’, proof that Picasso’s late work de­served more re­spect than the crit­ics of the time gave it.

shelf.title: Blue I, II and III
shelf.creator: Joan Miró
shelf.why: Very min­i­mal, yet in­cred­i­bly pow­er­ful in per­son.

shelf.title: Salvador Dali’s later work
shelf.creator: Salvador Dali
shelf.why: His later work ‘hit me re­ally hard’, with an as­sur­ance that blew Amit away.

shelf.title: The Push Man and Other Stories
shelf.creator: Yoshihiro Tatsumi
shelf.why: Gekiga at its best: dark urban sto­ries that stare into the depths of the human soul and go where manga doesn’t, in the vein Goya opened up cen­turies ear­lier.

shelf.title: Songs of Surrender
shelf.creator: U2
shelf.why: U2 re­think songs they wrote as kids from a more grown-up place, chang­ing ar­range­ments and lyrics in­stead of stay­ing frozen in the fa­mous ver­sions.

shelf.title: Time Out of Mind
shelf.creator: Bob Dylan
shelf.why: Amit’s favourite Dylan album, a prime ex­am­ple of late-career mas­tery.

shelf.title: Not Dark Yet
shelf.creator: Bob Dylan
shelf.why: ‘It’s not dark yet, but it’s get­ting there’ is an age­ing artist fac­ing mor­tal­ity and turn­ing it into art.

shelf.title: The Gate of Angels
shelf.creator: Penelope Fitzgerald
shelf.why: It is proof that great fic­tion can come very late in life.

shelf.title: Penelope Fitzgerald’s novels
shelf.creator: Penelope Fitzgerald
shelf.why: She wrote her first novel after 60, so ‘there is time for you to be a novelist’.

shelf.title: Perfect Days
shelf.creator: Wim Wenders
shelf.why: Wenders’s film pairs the striv­ing of sim­ply being at your work with mo­ments of si­lence and soli­tude we rarely get; Amit calls it ‘a film that could only be made by an old man’.

shelf.title: Paris, Texas
shelf.creator: Wim Wenders
shelf.why: Amit’s favourite Wim Wenders film, ‘such a masterpiece’, and his re­minder that great art comes young too.

shelf.title: Ramki and the Ocean of Stories (Episode 415 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It is the con­ver­sa­tion be­hind the shared ver­dict that Perfect Days could only be made by an older film­maker.

shelf.title: Life Lessons From Chess (Episode 81)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Lessons from chess on why re­newal mat­ters more than mas­tery (ex­perts in nar­row fields stop learn­ing), why young play­ers peak in a fi­nite game, and why a great firm re­cruits from all over the world.

shelf.title: The Story of Art
shelf.creator: EH Gombrich
shelf.why: Gombrich ex­plains the con­text and sto­ries be­hind works of art, paint­ing by paint­ing, so even peo­ple who re­spond to art only vis­cer­ally can un­der­stand it.

shelf.title: The Spirit of Indian Painting
shelf.creator: BN Goswamy
shelf.why: It does for Indian art what Gombrich does for art in gen­eral.

shelf.title: Ways of Seeing
shelf.creator: John Berger
shelf.why: Amit calls it a mas­ter­piece.

shelf.title: The Shock of the New
shelf.creator: Robert Hughes
shelf.why: Amit calls it a mas­ter­piece too.

laughs.text: Amit on the 27 Club fan­tasy: ‘when I was twenty one, I would fan­ta­size that I will die when I’m twenty seven after achiev­ing some­thing great. I achieved noth­ing great, so I post­poned it.’

Ajay’s ver­sion: he and Susan had a plan to do cool things by 29 and then give up, with no life be­yond 29. ‘And twenty nine came along and like we set­tled into a marathon.’ Amit, dead­pan: ‘You set­tled into a marathon.’
On Matisse tak­ing Les Demoiselles d’Avignon for a prank: if he’d had a Garmin watch, ‘he would prob­a­bly check it’ to see whether it was April 1.
After telling how a friend of Picasso shot him­self after try­ing to shoot the woman who spurned him: ‘And Picasso later sleeps with the woman, I think, but leave that aside later, later, not then.’

Amit’s rant at the critic who sneered at late Picasso: ‘Are you fuck­ing crazy? You’re a fuck­ing art critic who went to a uni­ver­sity and learned some­thing from some aca­demic fool. This is fuck­ing Picasso. Respect what he is doing.’

On why late bloomers in­spire him: ‘this feeds into my Bengali pro­cras­ti­na­tion. Because now I can think it I have wasted all my life so far, but I can waste twenty more years of it. Best work will hap­pen at 70, 80.’
Dylan, hos­pi­talised with peri­cardi­tis and sure he was dying: ‘I think I’m going to see Elvis soon.’

The fad­ing-light run­ning gag in an episode called The Light in Winter. The Dali chap­ter is dropped ‘be­cause I think we’ll run out of light’. On cut­ting the Miró chap­ter short: ‘Miró would not have ap­proved. Miró would have said I have cap­tured the fuck­ing light.’ And the sign-off: ‘The light has gone. I don’t even know if I’m vis­i­ble any­more... Are we au­di­ble? We are au­di­ble.’

After Ajay’s riff on what older minds are good for, Amit says: ‘the wis­dom that you just shared in the last five min­utes could not have been given by the twenty-year-old Ajay Shah. Am I cor­rect?’ Ajay: ‘Absolutely.’

Kurt Cobain’s ‘it’s bet­ter to burn out than to fade away’, and the rock stars who died at 27 (Janis Joplin, Jimi Hendrix, Jim Morrison), with 33 as ‘an­other age’ along­side Jesus Christ. Amit uses them as the myth of youth­ful ge­nius that the episode ar­gues against.
Bob Dylan’s line ‘he not busy being born is busy dying’ frames the whole episode: the Spanish mas­ters ‘were busy being born’ into old age.
Dylan going elec­tric and being branded Judas, used as the clas­sic case of fans who come to see ‘the pho­to­graph that Dylan left of himself’ rather than the man him­self.

On the Paris café cir­cles: ‘Imagine at your local BKC Starbucks, the great­est minds of the age gath­er­ing to­gether. But you don’t know they’re the great­est minds now. You’ll find out much later.’
Seeing Guernica in per­son is like ‘Lionel Messi is tak­ing a penalty in a World Cup final’, with a mass of peo­ple crowded in front of the giant can­vas.

Ajay re­calls John Maynard Keynes on Newton: ‘Newton was not just the first of the sci­en­tists, he was the last of the ma­gi­cians.’ Amit’s own image for Goya as a bridge be­tween worlds: ‘Oh my fuck­ing God he’s Istanbul.’
